title: Global Smartphone Shipments Plunge 22% in Record Quarterly Decline
summary:
Worldwide handset deliveries fell to 255.3 million units in the third quarter of 2026, according to data from IDC. Shipments dropped 22% year-over-year, marking the steepest quarterly contraction in the industry's history as AI data center demand diverted the supply of memory chips. These constraints drove component costs up approximately 350% since last year, forcing manufacturers to raise retail prices and reduce the availability of budget-tier models.

Chinese brands faced the most severe declines, with Xiaomi shipments falling 29.2% to 30.7 million units, Oppo dropping 34.5% to 25.6 million, and Vivo sliding 31.5% to 19.1 million. Samsung and Apple saw smaller decreases of 5.8% and 4.0% respectively by focusing on premium device segments. IDC Research Director Nabila Popal warned that the market has not yet reached its bottom and that growth may not recover until 2028 at the earliest.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
South Korea's stock market is in FREE FALL and the panic surrounding the memory trade is getting completely out of control.

The KOSPI just plunged another 7%, bringing its decline to roughly 40% from its June highs. Samsung and SK Hynix are getting absolutely destroyed, and the selling pressure is spreading across the entire AI infrastructure trade. I went on Making Money with @cvpayne today to talk about the memory selloff and why I believe investors are losing sight of what's actually happening in this industry.

And now we're getting ANOTHER warning out of South Korea. A new column published by Maeil Business Newspaper is raising concerns that the global memory industry could face oversupply beginning in 2029 as new manufacturing capacity starts coming online. The argument is that South Korea has become increasingly dependent on Samsung and SK Hynix, and that the country has roughly two to three years to develop other growth industries before the memory cycle potentially reverses. Now, I think this is something investors should absolutely pay attention to but here's where I disagree with the panic.

We're talking about a potential oversupply problem in 2029 while the industry is still struggling to meet demand TODAY. Memory manufacturers are already dealing with capacity constraints, AI customers are securing long term supply agreements, and demand for HBM continues to grow as Nvidia $NVDA and other AI chipmakers push toward increasingly memory intensive systems. And people need to understand that building additional manufacturing capacity doesn't automatically mean we're going to have an oversupply problem. These fabs take years to construct, equipment needs to be installed, production yields need to improve, and manufacturers still have to qualify their products with customers. Not to mention, HBM manufacturing is substantially more complicated than traditional DRAM, and not all additional memory capacity can immediately be used to produce the most advanced AI memory products.

Now, could we eventually see oversupply in 2029? ABSOLUTELY. Memory is a cyclical industry and I've never argued that these companies will enjoy record pricing and margins forever. But there's a massive difference between acknowledging that possibility and acting like the memory cycle is already over. I still believe the fundamentals of the memory trade remain incredibly strong, especially for companies positioned to benefit from HBM and the broader AI infrastructure buildout. selectedTweets.text:
🦔Global smartphone shipments fell 20% in the third quarter from a year ago, the weakest third quarter since 2012, according to Counterpoint Research. Memory chip prices shot up, phone makers passed the cost along, and phone prices are up about 20% this year.

My Take
AI data centers are outbidding regular people for memory chips. A basic DRAM chip that cost $6.30 a year ago went for about $26 at the end of September, and NAND storage runs about eight times what it did. Samsung posted a record $80 billion operating profit last quarter on the back of those prices, while phone sales shrink. It's basically an AI tax in the price of your next phone and laptop, even if you never touch a chatbot.

I don’t think it lasts forever. Memory booms usually end with too many factories, and China’s CXMT should have almost as much capacity as Micron by the end of this year. My guess is phone prices start easing sometime in 2027 once that supply shows up. Until then, a $90 battery replacement beats a $1,000 phone, and a lot of people are reaching the same conclusion.
